## Views

### Why Views?

Not everyone should see the full picture. Suppose someone needs an instructor's name and department, but **not** their salary. Instead of trusting every query to remember to hide the salary column, define it once:

```{.sql db="university"}
select id, name, dept_name from instructor;
```

A **view** is exactly this — a saved query that behaves like a "virtual table." It's not real stored data; it's a name attached to a query expression that gets substituted in wherever the view is used.

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>instructor</b></div><span>id, name, dept_name, salary</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>view</b></div><span>select id, name, dept_name</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>user query</b></div><span>sees only 3 columns</span></div></div>
```

### Creating a View

```sql
create view v as <query expression>;
```

```{.sql db="university"}
-- A view of instructors without salary
create or replace view faculty as
select id, name, dept_name from instructor;

-- Use it like a table
select name from faculty where dept_name = 'Biology';

-- A view with computed columns
create or replace view dept_salary_totals(dept_name, total_salary) as
select dept_name, sum(salary)
from instructor
group by dept_name;

select * from dept_salary_totals;
```

### Views Built on Views

Views can refer other views, not just base tables:

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace view physics_fall_2006 as
select course.course_id, sec_id, building, room_number
from course, section
where course.course_id = section.course_id
  and course.dept_name = 'Physics'
  and section.semester = 'Fall'
  and section.year = 2006;

create or replace view physics_fall_2006_taylor as
select course_id, room_number
from physics_fall_2006
where building = 'Taylor';

select * from physics_fall_2006_taylor;
```

- `v1` **depends directly on** `v2` if `v2` appears in `v1`'s definition.
- `v1` **depends on** `v2` if there's any chain of dependency leading from `v1` to `v2`.
- A view is **recursive** if it depends on itself.

### View Expansion

To understand what a nested view *really* means, SQL conceptually **expands** it: repeatedly replace each view name with its underlying query, until only base tables remain.

```
repeat:
    find a view reference v_i in the expression
    replace v_i with v_i's defining query
until no view references remain
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>physics_fall_2006_taylor</b></div><span>the query you write</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>physics_fall_2006</b></div><span>replaced by its definition</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>course, section</b></div><span>only base tables remain</span></div></div>
```

This terminates as long as no view is recursive.

### Updating Views

Inserting into a view secretly inserts into the underlying table:

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
insert into faculty values ('30765', 'Green', 'Biology');
-- Translates to:
-- insert into instructor values ('30765', 'Green', 'Biology', null);
select * from instructor where id = '30765';
rollback;
```

**But this only works cleanly for *simple* views** — most databases require:

- `from` clause has exactly **one** base table
- `select` lists plain column names only (no expressions, aggregates, or `distinct`)
- Any column left out of the `select` can default to `null`
- No `group by` or `having`

If a view joins multiple tables, an insert can be **ambiguous** (e.g., which department's row gets the new value if several departments share a building?) — and some inserts that satisfy the view's *output* can violate its `where` clause entirely, making the update meaningless to translate.

Try inserting into the `dept_salary_totals` view (it has `group by`), and the database refuses:

```{.sql db="university"}
insert into dept_salary_totals values ('Music', 100000);
```

### Materialized Views

A **materialized view** physically stores the view's result as a real table, instead of recomputing it on every query — faster to read, but it goes **stale** the moment the underlying tables change. Keeping it correct requires actively **maintaining** it (refreshing it) whenever the source data updates.

| View Type | Storage | Speed | Freshness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Regular View** | None (just a saved query) | Recomputed every time | Always current |
| **Materialized View** | Physical table | Fast to read | Needs manual/scheduled refresh |

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create materialized view dept_count as
select dept_name, count(*) as num_instructors
from instructor group by dept_name;

insert into instructor values ('30765', 'Green', 'Biology', 72000);
select * from dept_count where dept_name = 'Biology';   -- still the old count

refresh materialized view dept_count;
select * from dept_count where dept_name = 'Biology';   -- now updated
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>create</b></div><span>Biology: 2 stored</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>insert into instructor</b></div><span>table has 3, view still says 2</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>refresh</b></div><span>view shows 3</span></div></div>
```

## Transactions

A **transaction** is a unit of work — a group of one or more SQL statements that should succeed or fail *as a whole*.

- **Atomic**: either the *entire* transaction completes, or none of it does (rolled back as if it never happened).
- **Isolated**: a transaction shouldn't see the messy, half-finished state of another transaction running at the same time.
- Transactions begin **implicitly**, and end with either:
  - `commit work` — make all changes permanent
  - `rollback work` — undo everything since the transaction began

```{=html}
<div class="flow"><div class="box"><b>begin</b><span>start the unit of work</span></div><div class="box"><b>statements</b><span>queries and updates</span></div><div class="box"><b>commit work</b><span>make changes permanent</span></div><div class="box grey"><b>rollback work</b><span>undo everything</span></div></div>
```

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
update instructor set salary = salary * 1.10 where dept_name = 'Physics';
select name, salary from instructor where dept_name = 'Physics';   -- raised
rollback work;
select name, salary from instructor where dept_name = 'Physics';   -- back to the original
```

## Integrity Constraints

Constraints stop *valid-looking but wrong* changes from silently corrupting the database — e.g., "an instructor's salary must be greater than 29000" or "every instructor must have a name."

### On a Single Relation

| Constraint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `not null` | Column can never be empty |
| `primary key` | Uniquely identifies each row; implies `not null` + `unique` |
| `unique (A1, ..., Am)` | Columns form a **candidate key** — but unlike primary keys, candidate keys *can* be null |
| `check(P)` | Row must satisfy predicate `P` |

The university dataset already has these constraints. Each insert below breaks one of them, so the database rejects it:

```{.sql db="university"}
-- not null: name is required
insert into instructor values ('30767', null, 'Biology', 50000);
```

```{.sql db="university"}
-- check: salary > 29000
insert into instructor values ('30768', 'Low', 'Biology', 20000);
```

```{.sql db="university"}
-- check: semester in ('Fall', 'Winter', 'Spring', 'Summer')
insert into section values ('105', '9', 'Autumn', 2009, null, null, null);
```

Creating a new table with a `check` constraint (in the practice workspace):

```{.sql db="test_db"}
drop table if exists fixture;
create table fixture (
    match_num varchar(5),
    status varchar(10),
    primary key (match_num),
    check (status in ('Scheduled', 'Played', 'Postponed', 'Cancelled'))
);
insert into fixture values ('M0001', 'Played');      -- accepted
select * from fixture;
```

A value outside the list is rejected by the `check`:

```{.sql db="test_db"}
insert into fixture values ('M0002', 'Abandoned');
```

## Referential Integrity

Ensures a value referenced in one table **actually exists** in the table it points to. If `'Biology'` appears as a department name in `instructor`, there must be a matching row for `'Biology'` in `department`.

> **Formal definition:** If `A` is the primary key of relation `S`, then `A` is a **foreign key** of relation `R` if every value of `A` appearing in `R` also appears in `S`.

```{.sql db="university"}
-- 'Music' is not in department, so this is rejected
insert into instructor values ('30769', 'Lee', 'Music', 50000);
```

### Cascading Actions

What should happen when a referenced row is deleted or updated?

```{.sql db="test_db"}
drop table if exists project_cascade;
drop table if exists project;
drop table if exists department;

create table department (
    dept_name varchar(20) primary key,
    building varchar(15)
);

create table project (
    project_id char(5) primary key,
    title varchar(20),
    dept_name varchar(20) references department
);

-- with explicit cascading behavior
create table project_cascade (
    project_id char(5) primary key,
    title varchar(20),
    dept_name varchar(20),
    foreign key (dept_name) references department
        on delete cascade
        on update cascade
);
```

| Action | Effect when referenced row is deleted/updated |
|---|---|
| `cascade` | Automatically delete/update matching rows too |
| `no action` | Block the delete/update if references exist (default) |
| `set null` | Set the foreign key to `null` |
| `set default` | Set the foreign key to its default value |

The university dataset uses these actions. Deleting a department sets its instructors' `dept_name` to `null` (`set null`), and deleting a student removes their `takes` rows (`cascade`):

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
delete from department where dept_name = 'Biology';
select id, name, dept_name from instructor where id in ('80759', '81991');
rollback;
```

### The Chicken-and-Egg Problem

Self-referencing constraints can deadlock a single insert. Consider:

```sql
create table employee (
    id char(10),
    name char(40),
    manager_id char(10),
    primary key (id),
    foreign key (manager_id) references employee
);
```

How do you insert the very first employee if their manager must already exist? Three options:

1. Insert the manager *before* the employee who reports to them.
2. Set `manager_id` to `null` initially, then `update` it later (impossible if the column is `not null`).
3. **Defer** constraint checking until the transaction commits (covered in advanced topics).

## SQL Data Types and Schemas

### Built-in Date/Time Types

| Type | Stores | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `date` | Year, month, day | `date '2025-7-27'` |
| `time` | Hours, minutes, seconds | `time '09:00:30'` |
| `timestamp` | Date + time together | `timestamp '2025-7-27 09:00:30.75'` |
| `interval` | A span of time | `interval '1' day` |

::: {.callout-note title="Key idea"}
Subtracting two dates/times gives you an `interval`; adding an `interval` to a date/time shifts it forward or backward.
:::

```{.sql db="flis"}
select match_num, match_date,
       match_date + interval '7 days' as rematch_date,
       date '2020-12-31' - match_date as days_to_year_end
from matches;
```

### Indexes

An **index** is a shortcut structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.

```{.sql db="university"}
create index if not exists student_name_index on student(name);

select * from student where name = 'Manber';
-- with the index above, this skips a full table scan
```

### User-Defined Types (UDT)

Like a `typedef` in C — gives a meaningful name to an existing type.

```sql
create type dollars as numeric(12,2) final;

create table department (
    dept_name varchar(20),
    building varchar(15),
    budget dollars
);
```

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
This `create type … final` form is standard SQL and does not run in PostgreSQL. A **domain** (next) does the same job and runs on the dataset.
:::

### Domains

Similar to UDTs, but domains can carry their own **constraints**.

```{.sql db="test_db"}
drop table if exists visitor;
drop domain if exists person_name;
drop domain if exists member_kind;

create domain person_name varchar(20) not null;

create domain member_kind varchar(10)
    constraint member_kind_test
    check (value in ('Student', 'Faculty', 'Staff'));

create table visitor (name person_name, kind member_kind);
insert into visitor values ('Asha', 'Student');   -- accepted
select * from visitor;
```

A value the domain does not allow is rejected:

```{.sql db="test_db"}
insert into visitor values ('Ravi', 'Guest');
```

### Large Object Types

For storing big, unstructured content like photos, videos, or files:

| Type | Stores |
|---|---|
| `blob` | **B**inary **L**arge **OB**ject — raw binary data |
| `clob` | **C**haracter **L**arge **OB**ject — large character data |

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
A query returns a **pointer** to a large object, not the object itself — the actual data is fetched separately.
:::

## Authorization

### Forms of Authorization

**On data:**

| Privilege | Allows |
|---|---|
| `read` | Viewing data only |
| `insert` | Adding new rows |
| `update` | Modifying existing rows |
| `delete` | Removing rows |

**On schema:**

| Privilege | Allows |
|---|---|
| `index` | Creating/dropping indices |
| `resources` | Creating new relations |
| `alteration` | Adding/removing columns |
| `drop` | Deleting relations entirely |

### Granting Privileges

```sql
grant <privilege list> on <relation or view> to <user list>;
```

`<user list>` can be a specific user, `public` (everyone), or a **role**.

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create role u1;  create role u2;  create role admin_user;
grant select on instructor to u1, u2;
grant insert, update on course to u1;
grant all privileges on department to admin_user;
rollback;
```

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
The grantor must already **hold** the privilege themselves (or be the DBA). Granting a privilege on a *view* does **not** automatically grant privileges on the tables underneath it.
:::

### Revoking Privileges

```sql
revoke <privilege list> on <relation or view> from <user list>;
```

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create role u1;  create role u2;
grant select on department to u1, u2;
revoke select on department from u1, u2;
rollback;
```

- `revoke all from ...` removes every privilege the user holds.
- Revoking from `public` removes the privilege from everyone **except** users who were granted it explicitly elsewhere.
- If the same privilege was granted by **two different** grantors, revoking from one grantor may leave the privilege intact (granted by the other).
- Revoking a privilege also revokes any privileges that **depended** on it.

### Roles

Roles bundle privileges so you don't have to grant the same set repeatedly.

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>teaching_assistant</b></div><span>privileges of a TA</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>instructor</b></div><span>gets TA privileges too</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>dean</b></div><span>gets instructor and TA privileges</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>satoshi</b></div><span>inherits the whole chain</span></div></div>
```

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create role instructor_role;
create role amit;
grant select on takes to instructor_role;
grant instructor_role to amit;       -- amit inherits the privileges of 'instructor_role'

-- Roles can inherit from other roles
create role teaching_assistant;
grant teaching_assistant to instructor_role;   -- instructor_role now also gets TA's privileges

-- Chains of roles
create role dean;
create role satoshi;
grant instructor_role to dean;
grant dean to satoshi;          -- satoshi inherits dean → instructor_role → TA
rollback;
```

### Authorization on Views

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create view geo_instructors as
    (select * from instructor where dept_name = 'Geology');

create role geo_staff;
grant select on geo_instructors to geo_staff;
rollback;
```

If `geo_staff` queries `geo_instructors`, it works even if `geo_staff` has **no** direct permission on the underlying `instructor` table — the view's permissions are what matter, not the creator's original access (though if the view's *creator* lacked permission on `instructor`, the view itself couldn't have been created correctly in the first place).

### Other Authorization Features

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
create role mariano;  create role amit;  create role satoshi;

-- 'references' privilege needed to create a foreign key pointing at someone else's table
grant references (dept_name) on department to mariano;

-- Transferable privileges
grant select on department to amit with grant option;

-- Revoking with dependency handling
revoke select on department from amit, satoshi cascade;   -- also revokes anything amit/satoshi granted onward
rollback;
```

`revoke ... restrict` instead blocks the revoke if dependent privileges exist.

::: {.callout-note title="Key idea"}
The `references` privilege exists because a foreign key constraint can restrict what the *referenced* table's owner is allowed to do (e.g., blocking a delete due to `on delete no action`) — so creating that link requires explicit permission.
:::
